unit.title: Perform weld in flat and horizontal positions using gas tungsten metal arc welding process (GTAW) - (Tungsten inert gas - TIG)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In TIG welding, what does the tungsten electrode do?
options: It carries the arc and does not melt into the weld
It melts to become the filler metal in the joint
It holds the shielding gas inside the torch
It cools the weld pool so that it sets quickly

questions.stem: How is filler metal added in TIG welding?
options: It is fed automatically through the torch from a spool
It comes from the tungsten as it burns away
A filler rod is fed into the pool by the other hand
It is not possible to add filler metal in TIG

questions.stem: Why is TIG often chosen for thin sheet and stainless steel work?
options: It is the fastest process for thick structural steel
It gives fine control of heat and a clean, neat weld
It needs no shielding gas, so it is cheaper to run
It makes a heavy slag that protects thin metal

questions.stem: Which shielding gas is most often used for TIG welding steel, stainless steel and aluminium?
options: Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Argon mixed with 25% carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Pure argon

questions.stem: Why must carbon dioxide, or the argon and CO2 mixes used for MIG, never be used for TIG welding?
options: They are too heavy to flow through a TIG torch
They make the arc too cold to melt steel
They are only sold in small cylinders
They attack the hot tungsten and spoil the weld

questions.stem: Before you start a TIG job, where should you find the current, gas, tungsten and filler rod to use?
options: From whatever was used on the last job at the bench
From the welding procedure and the job drawing
From the colour of the plate you are welding
From the label on the side of the argon cylinder

questions.stem: Which argon flow rate is usual for TIG welding thin steel indoors with a standard cup?
options: About 1–2 litres per minute
About 40–50 litres per minute
About 7–12 litres per minute
About 80–100 litres per minute

questions.stem: Why does the gas keep flowing for a few seconds after the arc stops (post-flow)?
options: To protect the hot tungsten and weld from air as they cool
To blow the spatter off the weld so it looks clean
To empty the hose so that the cylinder can be changed
To cool the welder's hand inside the glove after welding

questions.stem: After welding, the tungsten is blue or black instead of bright silver. What does this usually mean?
options: The current was set exactly right for the job
The tungsten is new and has not been used before
The gas cover or post-flow was not enough
The filler rod was held too far from the pool

questions.stem: Which current and polarity is used for TIG welding carbon steel and stainless steel?
options: Alternating current (AC)
Direct current electrode negative (DCEN)
Direct current electrode positive (DCEP)
Any current, as polarity does not matter in TIG

questions.stem: Which current is normally used for TIG welding aluminium?
options: Alternating current (AC)
Direct current electrode negative (DCEN)
Direct current electrode positive (DCEP) only
No current, as aluminium can only be gas welded

questions.stem: Why is AC used for TIG welding aluminium?
options: Aluminium will not carry direct current
AC lets the tungsten melt into the weld as filler metal
AC needs no shielding gas on aluminium
It breaks up the tough oxide skin on the surface

questions.stem: With DCEN, where does most of the arc's heat go?
options: Into the tungsten electrode
Into the work piece
Into the filler rod only
Into the shielding gas

questions.stem: A tungsten electrode has a red band on its end. In the usual colour code, what type is it?
options: Pure tungsten
Zirconiated tungsten
2% thoriated tungsten
1.5% lanthanated tungsten

questions.stem: Which tungsten is traditionally used with AC on aluminium, where the end forms a small ball?
options: Pure or zirconiated tungsten
2% thoriated tungsten only
A carbon rod
A copper-coated steel rod

questions.stem: Thoriated tungsten contains a small amount of a radioactive material. What is the main precaution when grinding it?
options: Grind it only in the open air, away from any machines
Grind it quickly with no PPE so you breathe in less
Grind it on the same wheel as all other steel
Use extraction and a grinder kept for tungsten only

questions.stem: When grinding a tungsten to a point for DC welding, which way should the grinding marks run?
options: Around the tungsten, in rings
In a spiral from tip to collet
Along the length, towards the tip
It makes no difference which way

questions.stem: About how long should the ground taper (point) be on a tungsten for DC welding?
options: Exactly the same as the stick-out from the cup
About 2 to 2.5 times the tungsten's diameter
About 10 times the tungsten's diameter
No taper, as the end should be cut square

questions.stem: The tungsten touches the weld pool while you are welding. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as the arc will burn it clean
Turn up the current to melt off the dirt
Dip it in water to cool it down, then carry on welding
Stop, then grind off the dirty end and re-point it

questions.stem: Which part of the TIG torch grips the tungsten electrode?
options: The collet
The gas lens screen
The back cap
The ceramic cup

questions.stem: When you fit a tungsten in the torch, what must match the tungsten's diameter?
options: The length of the back cap
The collet and collet body
The size of the filler rod
The length of the torch cable

questions.stem: With a standard collet body, about how far should the tungsten stick out past the cup?
options: About 25–30 mm
Level with the cup, not sticking out
About 3–6 mm
About 15–20 mm

questions.stem: Two pieces of 1.5 mm steel sheet are to be TIG welded edge to edge (a butt joint). How should they be fitted up?
options: With a wide gap of about 5 mm for the rod to fill
Overlapped by 25 mm and clamped loosely
With a large bevel ground on each edge
Tight together, with no gap, and tacked often

questions.stem: Why is high-frequency (HF) or lift-arc starting used instead of scratching the tungsten on the plate?
options: Scratch starts can contaminate the tungsten and the weld
Scratching the plate makes the machine switch to AC
HF starting uses less argon than any other start
Scratching the plate always blunts the filler rod

questions.stem: Who should get advice before working near a TIG machine that uses high-frequency arc starting?
options: Anyone who wears glasses or contact lenses
Anyone who is left-handed and holds the torch differently
Anyone with a heart pacemaker or other implant
Anyone who has not eaten breakfast

questions.stem: TIG welding makes little smoke but strong ultraviolet light. What does this mean for PPE?
options: Skin can be left bare, since the arc is small
Skin and eyes need full cover, as with other arc welding
Only sunglasses are needed, as there is no spatter
Only a dust mask is needed, because there is no spatter to burn you

questions.stem: Which gloves are usually best for TIG welding?
options: Thin, close-fitting leather gloves for good feel
Thick rubber gloves used for cleaning
No gloves, so that you can feel the filler rod
Woollen gloves that are kept damp

questions.stem: TIG welding aluminium can make a lot of ozone. How should it be controlled?
options: Spray water into the air near the arc
Weld with the booth closed and the fan off
Open the argon valve wider to blow it away
Use local extraction and good general ventilation

questions.stem: Why must chlorinated degreasing solvents be kept away from the TIG arc?
options: They make the tungsten too hard to grind to a point afterwards
They make the filler rod melt too quickly
They stop the argon from flowing through the cup
The arc's light can turn their vapour into a poison gas

questions.stem: How should stainless steel be cleaned before TIG welding?
options: With the same steel wire brush that is used on rusty mild steel
With a file and some grease to stop rust
With a stainless brush kept for it, and a suitable solvent
It needs no cleaning, as stainless never gets dirty

questions.stem: Acetone is often used to wipe metal clean before TIG welding. Which precaution is right?
options: Keep it in an open tin beside the arc so it is handy
Use a little on a rag, let it dry, and keep it away from the arc
Pour it over the hot weld to cool it after welding
Mix it with water so that it works better

questions.stem: Which filler rod is normally used for TIG welding mild steel?
options: ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 steel rod
A 4043 aluminium rod
A copper-coated brazing rod
A flux-coated E6013 electrode

questions.stem: Where should the hot end of the filler rod be kept between dabs?
options: Lifted well above the cup, out of the way
Touching the tungsten, to keep it hot
Inside the gas shield, close to the pool
Laid on the bench beside the job

questions.stem: Where is the filler rod added to the weld pool?
options: At the front (leading) edge of the pool
Onto the tip of the tungsten
At the back of the pool, on the cooled weld
Into the arc, well above the pool

questions.stem: Which torch angle is normally used for TIG welding a butt joint in the flat position?
options: Flat along the plate, nearly touching it
Leaning back about 45° and pulling the torch towards you
Exactly upright, with no lean
About 10–20° from upright, pushing forward

questions.stem: At about what angle to the plate is the filler rod usually held?
options: About 90°, straight down into the pool
About 15–20°, low to the plate
About 60–70°, almost upright
Parallel to the torch, at the same angle

questions.stem: What is the usual arc length for TIG welding?
options: About the same as the tungsten diameter
About 25 mm, so that the pool is easy to see
Zero, with the tungsten touching the plate
As long as the arc can be held

questions.stem: On a TIG fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position, where should the torch point?
options: Straight at the upright plate, at 90°
Along the joint, flat on the bottom plate
About 45° between the plates, into the root
At the top edge of the upright plate, well above the root

questions.stem: Why should the current be brought down slowly (slope down or crater fill) at the end of a TIG weld?
options: To use up the last of the argon in the hose
To make the tungsten cool faster after welding
To burn off the oxide from the filler rod
To fill the crater and stop it cracking

questions.stem: What is a tungsten inclusion?
options: A tungsten that is far too long to fit inside the torch
A piece of tungsten left trapped in the weld
A crack along the centre of the weld
A ring of colour around the weld on steel

questions.stem: A TIG weld on steel shows porosity. Which is a likely cause?
options: A draught, too little gas or dirty metal
The tungsten was ground to a sharp point
The filler rod was clean and dry
The torch angle was 10–20° from upright

questions.stem: The back of a stainless steel TIG weld looks grey and crusty ("sugaring"). What caused it?
options: Too little filler rod was added, so the pool ran thin at the back
The tungsten had the wrong colour band
Air reached the hot back of the weld; it needed purging
The plate was cleaned before welding

questions.stem: What is the usual cause of undercut on a TIG weld?
options: A short arc and the correct current
Adding the filler rod at the front edge of the weld pool
Clean, dry metal and the correct gas flow
Too much heat, or too little filler at the edges

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a good TIG weld on carbon steel sheet?
options: A wide, flat bead with holes along the edges
Even ripples and width, fused at both edges
A tall, narrow bead with a black, sooty face
A dip in the centre where the plate has sunk

questions.stem: At the end of the day, what should be done with the argon supply and the TIG machine?
options: Close the cylinder, bleed the hose and switch off
Switch off at the wall and leave the cylinder open
Leave the machine on and the gas flowing for the next class
Unscrew the regulator while the cylinder is still open

essays.stem: Describe the PPE needed for TIG welding, and explain why skin and eye protection matter even though TIG makes little smoke or spatter.
essays.modelAnswer: TIG welding makes little smoke and almost no spatter, so it can look safe, but the arc gives off strong ultraviolet and infrared light, especially with argon and on aluminium. This light can burn the eyes, causing arc eye, and can burn bare skin like bad sunburn within minutes; long exposure can damage the skin. So a TIG welder wears a helmet with a filter shade suited to the current, often about shade 10 to 12 for normal work, and checks an auto-darkening helmet before use. Safety glasses are worn under the helmet for grinding tungsten and cleaning. Thin leather TIG gloves protect the hands while still giving fine control of the torch and rod. A flame-resistant, long-sleeved jacket buttoned at the neck covers the arms and chest, and the neck is covered too. Long trousers and safety boots protect the legs and feet from hot metal and falling parts. Screens protect other people from the arc light, and ventilation is still needed for ozone and fume.
markingPoints: Strong ultraviolet and infrared light even with little smoke: it burns eyes and skin
Helmet with a suitable shade (often about 10–12), checked before use; safety glasses under it for grinding
Thin leather TIG gloves for protection with good control
Flame-resistant long sleeves, neck covered, long trousers and safety boots
Screens for other people; ventilation for ozone and fume

essays.stem: Explain which current and polarity you would use for TIG welding carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: For carbon steel and stainless steel, TIG welding uses direct current electrode negative (DCEN). The tungsten is connected to the negative terminal and the work to the positive. With DCEN about two-thirds of the heat goes into the work and only about one-third into the tungsten, so the tungsten stays cool enough to keep its point, and the weld gets good, narrow penetration. For aluminium, alternating current (AC) is used. Aluminium is covered with a thin, tough oxide skin that melts at a much higher temperature than the metal underneath. During the electrode-positive half of each AC cycle the arc breaks up and cleans off this oxide, and during the electrode-negative half it puts heat into the work. Direct current electrode positive (DCEP) is hardly ever used for TIG, because most of the heat then goes into the tungsten, which would overheat and melt unless it were very thick. Always check the machine settings against the welding procedure before starting.
markingPoints: DCEN for carbon steel and stainless steel
DCEN puts most of the heat (about two-thirds) into the work, so the tungsten stays cool
AC for aluminium
The AC cleaning action breaks up the oxide skin
DCEP is rarely used because it overheats the tungsten

essays.stem: Describe how to choose, prepare and fit a tungsten electrode for TIG welding steel on DC.
essays.modelAnswer: First choose the type and size from the welding procedure. For DC work on steel, thoriated (red band), lanthanated or ceriated tungsten is common, and many centres now prefer lanthanated or ceriated types because thoriated tungsten is slightly radioactive. The diameter is chosen to suit the current, for example 1.6 mm or 2.4 mm for thin sheet. Grind the end to a point on a grinder kept only for tungsten, with the extraction on and safety glasses worn. Hold the tungsten so that the grinding marks run along its length towards the tip, not around it, because this gives a steady arc. Make the taper about 2 to 2.5 times the diameter long, and leave a very small flat on the tip so that it does not break off into the weld. Fit a collet and collet body of the same size as the tungsten, put the tungsten in, set it to stick out about 3–6 mm past the cup, and tighten the back cap by hand. Check that the cup size suits the job.
markingPoints: Chooses the type and size from the procedure, suited to DC, and knows the thoriated hazard
Grinds on a wheel kept for tungsten, with extraction and eye protection
Grinding marks along the length; taper about 2–2.5 times the diameter; small flat on the tip
Collet and collet body matched to the tungsten size
Correct stick-out (about 3–6 mm) and the back cap tightened

essays.stem: Explain the job of the shielding gas in TIG welding, and describe how you would set it up and check it.
essays.modelAnswer: The shielding gas, usually pure argon, flows out of the cup and keeps the air away from the hot tungsten, the weld pool and the hot end of the filler rod. Without it, oxygen and nitrogen in the air would burn the tungsten and cause porosity and oxidation in the weld. To set it up, check that the cylinder label says argon, chain the cylinder upright, and fit the correct argon regulator/flowmeter, with clean, undamaged threads and no oil. Stand to the side and open the valve slowly, then check the joints with leak-detection fluid. Press the torch switch or gas test button and set the flow, usually about 7–12 litres per minute for a standard cup indoors. Set the pre-flow to clear the torch before the arc starts, and the post-flow so that gas keeps covering the tungsten and the weld as they cool. Screen the work from fans and draughts. A bright, silver tungsten after welding shows that the gas cover was good; a blue or black one shows it was not.
markingPoints: Argon keeps air off the tungsten, pool and rod, preventing porosity and oxidation
Cylinder label checked, cylinder chained, correct regulator fitted, valve opened slowly
Joints leak-tested with fluid
Flow set (about 7–12 L/min), with pre-flow and post-flow set
Work screened from draughts; tungsten colour used as a check

essays.stem: Describe how to make a TIG butt weld on 1.5 mm to 2 mm carbon steel sheet in the flat position, including the torch and filler rod angles.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean the sheet edges back to bright metal and wipe off any oil. Fit the pieces tightly together with no gap, and tack them at each end and at short distances along the joint so that they do not move. Set DCEN, a pointed tungsten, the argon flow and a current to suit the thickness, from the procedure. Hold the torch about 10–20° from upright, leaning in the direction of travel so that you push the pool along, and keep a short arc about the same length as the tungsten diameter. Wait for a small, shiny pool to form across both edges. Hold the filler rod at about 15–20° to the sheet and dab it into the front edge of the pool, then move the torch forward a little and repeat, in an even rhythm. Keep the hot end of the rod inside the gas shield, and never let the tungsten touch the pool or the rod. At the end, slope the current down or ease off the pedal to fill the crater, and hold the torch still while the post-flow covers the weld.
markingPoints: Edges cleaned, fitted tight and tacked at short distances
Torch about 10–20° from upright, pushing, with a short arc
Rod at about 15–20°, dabbed into the front of the pool in a steady rhythm
Hot end of the rod kept in the gas; tungsten kept off the pool and rod
Crater filled and the post-flow held over the weld at the end

essays.stem: Explain why cleanliness is so important in TIG welding, and describe how to keep the work, filler rod and tungsten clean.
essays.modelAnswer: TIG welding has no flux, so nothing in the process cleans the metal. Any oil, grease, paint, rust, moisture or dirt goes straight into the weld and causes porosity, poor fusion, cracks and a dirty finish. A dirty tungsten gives a wandering arc and can drop pieces into the weld. So clean the work back to bright metal with a grinder, file or wire brush. Use a stainless steel brush kept only for stainless steel, or only for aluminium, so that you do not carry bits of mild steel that cause rust or contamination. Wipe the joint with a clean cloth and a suitable solvent such as acetone, let it dry fully, and keep the solvent away from the arc. Never use chlorinated solvents near welding. Keep filler rods in their packet or tube, wipe them before use, and do not handle them with greasy gloves. If the tungsten touches the pool or the rod, stop, grind off the dirty end and re-point it on the tungsten grinder. Keep gloves clean and dry.
markingPoints: No flux, so dirt goes straight into the weld: porosity, poor fusion, cracks
Work cleaned to bright metal, with separate brushes for stainless steel and aluminium
Solvent wipe, allowed to dry, kept away from the arc; no chlorinated solvents
Filler rods kept clean in their packet and wiped before use
A dirty tungsten is stopped, ground off and re-pointed

essays.stem: Name four defects that can happen in TIG welds. For each one, give a cause and a way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Tungsten inclusion is a piece of tungsten trapped in the weld. It is caused by touching the tungsten into the pool or the rod, or by too much current for the tungsten size. Prevent it by keeping a steady, short arc, using the right size of tungsten and re-pointing it if it gets dirty. Porosity is gas holes in the weld, caused by too little gas, a draught, a leak, or dirty metal or rod. Prevent it by setting the flow correctly, screening the work and cleaning the metal and rod. Undercut is a groove at the edge of the weld, caused by too much current or not adding enough filler at the edges. Prevent it by lowering the current and adding rod at the right time. Crater cracks are small cracks at the end of the weld, caused by stopping the arc suddenly. Prevent them by sloping the current down or using crater fill, and adding a little rod at the end. Sugaring on the back of stainless steel is caused by poor gas cover; prevent it with good gas cover and back purging.
markingPoints: Names four real TIG defects (for example tungsten inclusion, porosity, undercut, crater cracks, sugaring)
Gives a correct cause for each
Gives a correct way to prevent each
Links the causes to gas cover, cleanliness, current and technique

essays.stem: Apart from the arc light, describe the health and safety hazards of TIG welding and how each is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Electric shock: the torch and leads carry welding current, so check the cables for damage, keep gloves and clothing dry, and never weld standing in water. High-frequency arc starting can affect pacemakers and nearby electronics, so people with implants must take medical advice, and the maker's instructions must be followed. Ozone and fume: the arc's ultraviolet light makes ozone, especially on aluminium, so use local extraction and good ventilation. Argon is heavier than air and can collect in low or closed spaces and push out the oxygen, so close the valve when not in use and never weld in a closed space without proper controls. Thoriated tungsten grinding dust is slightly radioactive, so use a grinder kept for tungsten with extraction, or use a non-thoriated type. Acetone can catch fire, and chlorinated solvents can make a poison gas near the arc, so keep solvents away from welding. Gas cylinders must be chained upright. Hot metal causes burns, so use pliers and mark hot work. Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Electric shock and high-frequency start (pacemakers), with controls
Ozone and fume controlled with extraction and ventilation
Argon build-up in low or closed spaces, and how to prevent it
Thoriated tungsten dust controlled, or a non-thoriated type used
Solvent fire and poison gas, cylinders chained, hot metal handled safely

essays.stem: Describe how to make a TIG fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position on 3 mm carbon steel, and how you would check it.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean both plates to bright metal and wipe them with solvent. Tack the upright plate square on the base plate with small tacks at each end and in the middle. Set DCEN, a pointed tungsten, the argon flow and the current from the procedure, and test on scrap. Because the tungsten must reach into the root, a little more stick-out may be needed, as long as the gas still covers it. Point the torch at about 45° between the plates, into the root, and lean it about 10–20° in the direction of travel. Form a pool that melts into both plates equally. Add the filler rod at the front of the pool, mostly towards the upper edge, so that the weld does not sag onto the bottom plate and leave undercut on the upright plate. Move steadily so that the legs stay equal, and fill the crater at the end. When the weld is cool, check the legs with a fillet gauge, and look for even ripples, smooth toes, no undercut, no porosity and good fusion into the root.
markingPoints: Plates cleaned and tacked square
Settings from the procedure and tested; enough stick-out to reach the root with gas cover
Torch about 45° between the plates with a 10–20° lean in the direction of travel
Rod added at the front of the pool, towards the upper edge, to avoid sag and undercut
Crater filled; legs checked with a fillet gauge and the weld checked by eye

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make on a TIG set before welding, and what you would do at the end of the job.
essays.modelAnswer: Before welding, check the mains cable and plug for damage, and that the machine has a current test tag if the Centre uses them. Check the torch cable, the work lead and the clamp for cuts, burns and loose connections. Check the cup for cracks and chips, and that the collet, collet body and back cap match the tungsten size and are tight. Check that the tungsten is clean, correctly pointed and the right type for the job. Check that the argon cylinder is chained, the hose is not cracked and the joints do not leak. Check that the foot pedal or torch switch works, and set the current, polarity, pre-flow and post-flow for the job. At the end of the job, close the cylinder valve, bleed the gas from the hose and switch the machine off. Let the torch cool, then coil the cables neatly off the floor. Put tungstens and rods back in their boxes, clean the bench and sweep up. Report any fault to the instructor and tag faulty equipment out of use.
markingPoints: Checks the mains cable, torch cable, work lead and clamp
Checks the cup, collet, collet body, back cap and tungsten
Checks the cylinder, hose and joints, the pedal or switch, and the settings
At the end: valve closed, gas bled, machine off, cables coiled, consumables stored
Reports faults and tags faulty equipment out of use

practical1.title: TIG butt and lap welds in the flat position (1G and 1F) on thin carbon steel sheet
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a TIG station safely for DCEN welding of carbon steel. Together, check the machine, torch, leads and argon supply, and set the gas flow, pre-flow and post-flow. Each member grinds and fits their own tungsten (correct taper, matching collet, correct stick-out) while the assessor watches, then makes one square-edge butt weld in the flat position (1G) and one lap fillet weld in the flat position (1F) in 1.5 mm or 2 mm carbon steel sheet, each about 100 mm long, adding ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 filler rod. Each member checks their own welds front and back, and marks any faults. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every member has welded and the area is clean.
materials: 1.5 mm or 2 mm carbon steel sheet: 4 pieces of about 100 mm × 40 mm for each member
1.6 mm or 2.4 mm tungsten electrodes (lanthanated or ceriated preferred)
1.6 mm ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 filler rod
TIG machine with torch, matching collets and collet bodies, cups and foot pedal
Tungsten grinder with extraction, stainless wire brush, acetone and clean rags
Clamps, pliers, steel rule and chalk
photos: The TIG station set up: cylinder chained, screens in place, every member in full PPE
A ground tungsten next to a rule, showing the length of the taper
The tungsten fitted in the torch, showing the stick-out past the cup
Butt joint fitted tight and tacked
Each member's finished butt weld, front and back, labelled with their name
Each member's finished lap weld, labelled with their name
The work area cleaned, cylinder closed and cables coiled
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout, including safety glasses when grinding the tungsten
Ground the tungsten with the marks along its length and a taper of about 2–2.5 times the diameter
Fitted the tungsten with the matching collet and a correct stick-out
Fitted the sheet tight and tacked it at short distances
Kept a short arc and dabbed the rod into the front of the pool, keeping the rod end in the gas
Did not let the tungsten touch the pool or rod; re-pointed it if it did
Butt weld fused at both edges with penetration on the back; lap weld fused into both pieces
Left the station safe: cylinder closed, hose bled, tungstens and rods put away
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens; TIG gives strong ultraviolet light even with little smoke
Grind tungsten only on the grinder kept for it, with extraction on and safety glasses worn
Keep acetone and rags away from the arc; never use chlorinated solvents near welding
Keep the argon cylinder upright and chained; close it when not in use
Anyone with a pacemaker or implant must take advice before working near high-frequency start
Treat all metal as hot: use pliers and mark hot work

practical2.title: TIG fillet welds on tee joints in the horizontal position (2F), 3 mm carbon steel
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare and TIG weld tee joints in 3 mm carbon steel plate in the horizontal position (2F). Each member cleans and tacks the parts for one side of a tee joint, makes a test weld on scrap, and then welds one side of a tee joint (about 100 mm long) while the assessor watches. The group will need 2 or 3 tee joints. Each member checks their own weld with a fillet gauge, and another member checks it again. As a group, fill in a simple inspection sheet for every weld (leg size, ripples, undercut, porosity, fusion). Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every member has welded and the area is clean.
materials: 6 pieces of 3 mm carbon steel plate, about 100 mm × 50 mm (for 3 tee joints)
Scrap plate of the same thickness for test welds
2.4 mm tungsten electrodes (lanthanated or ceriated preferred)
2.4 mm ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 filler rod
TIG machine with torch, cups, collets and foot pedal
Fillet weld gauge, try square, stainless wire brush, acetone and clean rags
photos: Plates cleaned to bright metal, ready to tack
Tee joints tacked square, with a try square in place
A test weld on scrap, with the current setting written beside it
Each member's finished fillet weld, labelled with their name
End view of a joint, showing both legs
The fillet gauge on a finished weld
The work area cleaned, cylinder closed and cables coiled
checklist: Cleaned the plates and tacked the tee joint square
Set and tested the current on scrap before welding the joint
Held the torch at about 45° between the plates with a slight lean in the direction of travel
Added rod at the front of the pool towards the upper plate, with no undercut on the upright plate
Finished fillet: equal legs, even ripples, smooth toes, no porosity
Checked a weld with the fillet gauge and filled in the inspection sheet
Left the station safe and tidy, with the cylinder closed and the hose bled
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before you strike an arc
Use the fume extraction and keep the booth ventilated for ozone
Keep acetone and rags away from the arc and from hot metal
Keep gloves and clothing dry; check the torch and leads for damage before use
Keep the argon cylinder upright and chained; close it when not in use
Treat all metal as hot: use pliers and mark hot work
